newsitem.title: USA: Boeing, McDonnell Douglas shares surge.
newsitem.headline: Boeing, McDonnell Douglas shares surge.

text.p: The shares of Boeing Co. and McDonnell Douglas Corp. soared Monday in early trading as Wall Street applauded the $13.3 billion merger of the rival aerospace giants.
Boeing traded at $102.50, up $5.75, and McDonnell Douglas leaped $12.25 to $64.25, both on the New York Stock Exchange.
Boeing and McDonnell announced Sunday that McDonnell would be acquired by Boeing in an exchange of stock.
With a projected total of $48 billion in combined annual revenue, the company would rank about 10th on the Fortune 500, Fortune Magazine's annual list of the world's largest corporations.
"This is the deal we wanted and we are very happy with it," Harry Stonecipher, chief executive officer of McDonnell Douglas, said Monday in an interview on CNBC Television.
Stonecipher will become chief operating officer of the merged company and Phil Condit, CEO of Boeing, will become chairman.
"It's a great deal for Boeing and a good way out for McDonnell Douglas," said a Wall Street trader who spoke on condition of not being named.

"McDonnell Douglas just didn't have the resources to aggressively fund its development programmes," said Nick Heymann, an analyst at Natwest Securities. "They got stretched too thin on transports and fighters and commercial and they underinvested."
McDonnell Douglas decided in October to abandon development of the MD-XX widebody commercial jet, and in November it lost a U.S. military contract for a jet fighter worth potentially $200 billion.
Currently, McDonnell Douglas employs 65,000 people, including 24,000 in St. Louis, where it is based, down from a peak of about 136,000 at the start of the decade.
Analysts said McDonnell Douglas had few options without the merger and would have been likely to become a niche player producing cargo aircraft for the commercial and military markets.
"This was done on Boeing's terms, for Boeing's benefit and will ultimately solve a lot of the problems of McDonnell Douglas," Heymann said.
The surge in Boeing's shares contributed to a sharp rally on Wall Street, where the Dow Jones industrial average jumped 50 points in early trading.
The proposed merger also reverberated in Europe, where rival aircraft maker Airbus Industrie weighed the repercussions on its business.

Airbus is a partnership of French state-owned Ste Nationale Industrielle Aerospatiale; British Aerospace Plc; Daimler-Benz Aerospace, a unit of Daimler-Benz AG; and Construcciones Aeronauticas SA of Spain.
The merger put new urgency on the consortium's plan to restructure itself into a company that could rival the new U.S. titan.
Historically, Boeing has held about 60 percent of the world civilian aircraft market, Airbus 30 percent and McDonnell Douglas 10 percent.
